[Section: Reclassifying rasters, Page: 312, Source: data/uploads/bf2804feea57434bb79b749134ed1df0_QGIS-3.44-TrainingManual-en.pdf]
QGIS Training Manual
1. Open the layer Properties dialog (as usual, via the right-click menu of the layer)
2. Click on the Symbology tab
3. Where it says Singleband gray (in the Render type dropdown menu), change it to Singleband pseudocolor
4. Choose Mean +/- standard deviation x for Min / Max Value Settings with a value of 2.0
5. Select a suitable Color ramp
6. Click Run
8.4.13 Try Yourself: Aspect
Use the same approach as for calculating the slope, choosing Aspect… in the Raster ► Analysis menu.
Remember to save the project periodically.
8.4.14 Reclassifying rasters
1. Choose Raster ► Raster calculator…
2. Specify your Rasterprac directory as the location for the Output layer (click on the … button), and save it
as slope15_60.tif
3. Ensure that the Open output file after running algorithm box is selected.
In the Raster bands list on the left, you will see all the raster layers in your Layers panel. If your Slope layer is
called slope, it will be listed as slope@1. Indicating band 1 of the slope raster.
4. The slope needs to be between 15 and 60 degrees.
Using the list items and buttons in the interface, build the following expression:
(slope@1 > 15) AND (slope@1 < 60)
5. Set the Output layer field to an appropriate location and file name.
6. Click Run.
Fig. 8.8: Raster calculator Slope
Now find the correct aspect (east-facing: between 45 and 135 degrees) using the same approach.
1. Build the following expression:
(aspect@1 > 45) AND (aspect@1 < 135)
You will know it worked when all of the east-facing slopes are white in the resulting raster (it’s almost as if they are
being lit by the morning sunlight).
Find the correct rainfall (greater than 1000 mm) the same way. Use the following expression:
Rainfall30@1 > 1000
Now that you have all three criteria each in separate rasters, you need to combine them to see which areas satisfy all
the criteria. To do so, the rasters will be multiplied with each other. When this happens, all overlapping pixels with
a value of 1 will retain the value of 1 (i.e. the location meets the criteria), but if a pixel in any of the three rasters
has the value of 0 (i.e. the location does not meet the criteria), then it will be 0 in the result. In this way, the result
will contain only the overlapping areas that meet all of the appropriate criteria.
298 Chapter 8. Module: Completing the Analysis

1. Open the layer Properties dialog (as usual, via the right-click menu of the layer)
2. Click on the Symbology tab
3. Where it says Singleband gray (in the Render type dropdown menu), change it to Singleband pseudocolor
4. Choose Mean +/- standard deviation x for Min / Max Value Settings with a value of 2.0
5. Select a suitable Color ramp

8.4.13 Try Yourself: Aspect
Use the same approach as for calculating the slope, choosing Aspect… in the Raster ► Analysis menu.
Remember to save the project periodically.
8.4.14 Reclassifying rasters
1. Choose Raster ► Raster calculator…
2. Specify your Rasterprac directory as the location for the Output layer (click on the … button), and save it
as slope15_60.tif
3. Ensure that the Open output file after running algorithm box is selected.
In the Raster bands list on the left, you will see all the raster layers in your Layers panel. If your Slope layer is
called slope, it will be listed as slope@1. Indicating band 1 of the slope raster.
4. The slope needs to be between 15 and 60 degrees.
Using the list items and buttons in the interface, build the following expression:
(slope@1 > 15) AND (slope@1 < 60)
5. Set the Output layer field to an appropriate location and file name.
6. Click Run.
Fig. 8.8: Raster calculator Slope
Now find the correct aspect (east-facing: between 45 and 135 degrees) using the same approach.
1. Build the following expression:
(aspect@1 > 45) AND (aspect@1 < 135)
You will know it worked when all of the east-facing slopes are white in the resulting raster (it’s almost as if they are
being lit by the morning sunlight).
Find the correct rainfall (greater than 1000 mm) the same way. Use the following expression:
Rainfall30@1 > 1000
Now that you have all three criteria each in separate rasters, you need to combine them to see which areas satisfy all
the criteria. To do so, the rasters will be multiplied with each other. When this happens, all overlapping pixels with
a value of 1 will retain the value of 1 (i.e. the location meets the criteria), but if a pixel in any of the three rasters
has the value of 0 (i.e. the location does not meet the criteria), then it will be 0 in the result. In this way, the result
will contain only the overlapping areas that meet all of the appropriate criteria.

1. Open the layer Properties dialog (as usual, via the right-click menu of the layer)
2. Click on the Symbology tab
3. Where it says Singleband gray (in the Render type dropdown menu), change it to Singleband pseudocolor
4. Choose Mean +/- standard deviation x for Min / Max Value Settings with a value of 2.0
5. Select a suitable Color ramp
6. Click Run
8.4.13 Try Yourself: Aspect
Use the same approach as for calculating the slope, choosing Aspect… in the Raster ► Analysis menu.
Remember to save the project periodically.
8.4.14 Reclassifying rasters
1. Choose Raster ► Raster calculator…
2. Specify your Rasterprac directory as the location for the Output layer (click on the … button), and save it
as slope15_60.tif
3. Ensure that the Open output file after running algorithm box is selected.
In the Raster bands list on the left, you will see all the raster layers in your Layers panel. If your Slope layer is
called slope, it will be listed as slope@1. Indicating band 1 of the slope raster.
4. The slope needs to be between 15 and 60 degrees.
Using the list items and buttons in the interface, build the following expression:
(slope@1 > 15) AND (slope@1 < 60)
5. Set the Output layer field to an appropriate location and file name.
6. Click Run.
Fig. 8.8: Raster calculator Slope
Now find the correct aspect (east-facing: between 45 and 135 degrees) using the same approach.
1. Build the following expression:
(aspect@1 > 45) AND (aspect@1 < 135)
You will know it worked when all of the east-facing slopes are white in the resulting raster (it’s almost as if they are
being lit by the morning sunlight).
Find the correct rainfall (greater than 1000 mm) the same way. Use the following expression:
Rainfall30@1 > 1000
Now that you have all three criteria each in separate rasters, you need to combine them to see which areas satisfy all
the criteria. To do so, the rasters will be multiplied with each other. When this happens, all overlapping pixels with
a value of 1 will retain the value of 1 (i.e. the location meets the criteria), but if a pixel in any of the three rasters
has the value of 0 (i.e. the location does not meet the criteria), then it will be 0 in the result. In this way, the result
will contain only the overlapping areas that meet all of the appropriate criteria.

a value of 1 will retain the value of 1 (i.e. the location meets the criteria), but if a pixel in any of the three rasters
has the value of 0 (i.e. the location does not meet the criteria), then it will be 0 in the result. In this way, the result
will contain only the overlapping areas that meet all of the appropriate criteria.

- Each candidate describes a SCREEN STATE — the state of the UI when that step is the user's current position (its expected dialog, expected elements and keywords describe what the screen shows at that point). Pick the candidate whose described state matches the CURRENT screen. Do NOT pick the step whose action the user is about to perform: the next action is supplied later from the workflow edges.
- Candidates that share the same dialog are told apart by FIELD VALUES in visual_state (field_values / labels): the selected dropdown entry, whether a text field is filled or empty, whether a checkbox is checked, whether a list is empty. A label merely being visible on screen (e.g. an unchecked checkbox or an empty field with its caption) is NOT evidence for a candidate that requires it to be set.
- Prefer a candidate from the same workflow as the session's previous steps and the graph prior, unless the screen clearly shows a different application module.
- Return "none" when NO candidate is even loosely related (different application, different module, totally unrelated topic).

CONFIDENCE (recorded, not used as a gate; below 0.70 is treated as unsure):
- 0.9–1.0: the candidate's dialog AND its field states are literally on screen.
- 0.7–0.85: same dialog/workflow, field states consistent but not all visible.
- 0.5–0.65: plausible topic only. Use this when unsure; do NOT inflate.

NOTE — steps that span several actions and dialogs that stay open:
- A step may cover several actions; the screen still matches that step until its completion state (as described by its successor) is visible.
- Pick the SUCCESSOR only if the screen shows the successor's described state (its field values are now set). If the instructions already given completed a step but the screen has not changed, stay on that step.
